open-question.question: CONTRIBUTING.md (## Development) and SECURITY.md each say "both" hosts or repositories and name the two, but neither appears in the Goal's release-ready surface list nor in any decision. Do they gain Codex wording in this milestone?
open-question.recommendation: Both files keep their current style and become correct in the same milestone that commits the Codex tree, with no release-skill step to maintain. The cairn-codex links start resolving on their own when the repository is created at the first Codex release, and the root README's install section already names that repository over the same window; this differs from the adoption-table badge, which would stay broken until a seed run and so needed a follow-up.
open-question.alternative: Both files gain Codex wording inside this milestone, keeping their current style of naming every host and repository. Only the sentences that list hosts or repositories change. In CONTRIBUTING.md (## Development), "supports both Claude Code and Google Antigravity" becomes a three-host sentence. The definition-directory list adds `scripts/hosts/codex/`, the committed-tree list adds `hosts/codex/`, and the distribution-repository sentence adds a `cairn-codex` link. In SECURITY.md, "both distribution repositories" becomes all three, with a `cairn-codex` link beside the other two. Every root document matches the three-host project as soon as the Codex tree is committed. The fix sits in the same milestone as the rest of the release-ready surface, and these root files are outside `hosts/`, so it can't touch the byte-identity bar. The `cairn-codex` links in both files point at a repository that doesn't exist until the first Codex release, because the "Distribution repository creation" decision leaves it uncreated. A reader following them before then reaches a 404. The next host added will need these same sentences edited again.

Both files are rewritten inside this milestone so they name no host and no repository. Each sentence that lists hosts, definition directories, committed trees or distribution repositories is replaced by a general statement. Examples: every host defined under `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, each rendered into `hosts/<host>/`, and each published to its own `uHappyLogic/cairn-<host>` repository as listed in the README's installation section. SECURITY.md likewise says fixes ship to every distribution repository instead of "both" plus two links. No Codex-specific text is added. Neither file is wrong at any point: not when the Codex tree lands, not before `cairn-codex` exists, and not after. No later host needs these files edited again, which matches how the release skill already finds hosts without naming any. Readers lose the direct repository links, and CONTRIBUTING loses the concrete note that `cairn-claude` is the recommended install source. They are sent to the README instead. The rewrite also touches more prose than adding a third name would.

Both files are edited inside this milestone, and each kind of mention is handled separately. open-question.question: The "Codex plugin-root literal" decision says the build stays unchanged, but the build's dangling-plugin-root check resolves every plugin-root reference against the host tree's root, and the "Codex install route" decision puts the plugin under plugins/cairn/, so every ${PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/ and ${PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/ reference in the Codex tree would name no file and fail the gate. How does the build validate plugin-root references for a host whose plugin root is a subdirectory of its tree?
open-question.recommendation: A declared key keeps the check exactly as strict for Codex as for the other two hosts and changes only the check's resolution base, so the rendering code is untouched and the byte-identity bar is not put at risk. Layout values, renames and template paths all stay relative to the tree root, which gives a definition one frame of reference, and the plugin root is stated in the definition instead of inferred by a hidden rule; the prefix written twice is guarded by definition validation.
open-question.alternative: The build gains one more settings key, for example `plugin_dir`: the path from the host tree's root to the directory that `plugin_root` stands for at runtime. Every definition declares it. Claude Code and Antigravity set it to the empty string, and Codex sets it to `plugins/cairn`. The fixed key set grows by this one key, and a missing or unknown key is still a build error. `[layout]`, `renames` and template paths stay relative to the tree root, so the Codex layout still says `plugins/cairn/skills` and so on. The `dangling-plugin-root` check resolves each `${PLUGIN_ROOT}/<path>` reference against `tree/plugin_dir` instead of `tree`, and otherwise works as today. Definition validation also fails when any layout value falls outside `plugin_dir`. The check's line in the docstring and the settings comment explain the key. The "Codex plugin-root literal" decision's "build stays unchanged" clause is amended to cover this check only. The check stays exactly as strict as it is for the other two hosts: every Codex reference must name a real file at the path `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` resolves to at runtime. The plugin root is stated in one declarative place, in the same style as the other keys. `settings.toml` is not rendered into any tree, so the Claude Code and Antigravity trees stay byte-identical. The `plugins/cairn` prefix is written twice in the Codex definition, in `plugin_dir` and in every layout value. That needs a new consistency rule in definition validation. All three definitions must change to declare a key that two of them leave empty. Whether the key also governs where the Codex manifest template renders belongs to the "Manifest template path" question, so its scope depends on how that question is answered.

alternative.id: Plugin-dir key, layout relative to it

open-question.alternative: The build gains the same declared `plugin_dir` key, empty for Claude Code and Antigravity and `plugins/cairn` for Codex. In this option, though, `[layout]` values become relative to `plugin_dir`, so all three definitions keep writing `skills = "skills"` and so on, and the build adds the prefix when it places files. The `dangling-plugin-root` check resolves references against `tree/plugin_dir`. `renames` and templates stay relative to the tree root. Docstring and settings comments are updated, and the "build stays unchanged" clause is amended to cover this change. The plugin root is stated once, with nothing to keep in sync. The check is just as strict as in the option above. The Codex definition's layout reads like the other two, so plugin placement and plugin-root resolution cannot disagree by construction. The meaning of `[layout]` changes for every host, and the build's placement code changes, not only its check. Definitions then use two reference frames: layout relative to the plugin directory, and `renames` and templates relative to the tree root. That mismatch invites mistakes. Rendering also changes, so the strict byte-identity bar has to catch any slip in the Claude Code and Antigravity trees. Whether templates follow `plugin_dir` belongs to the "Manifest template path" question.

No new settings key. The build derives each host's plugin-root directory as the longest common parent directory of its `[layout]` values. That is empty for Claude Code and Antigravity, whose layouts map to `skills`, `agents`, `shared` and `tools` at the tree root, and `plugins/cairn` for Codex. The `dangling-plugin-root` check resolves references against that derived directory. The docstring states the derivation rule. The settings key set and all three definitions stay as they are, and the "build stays unchanged" clause is amended to cover only the check's resolution base. The change is smallest and confined to one function. No definition changes, the fixed key set is untouched, and the prefix is never written twice. The check stays strict for the layouts all three hosts actually use. The base comes from a hidden rule, not a declared value. A future layout whose directories do not share the plugin root as their common parent would make the check validate against the wrong directory without any warning. For example, a host might place `tools` elsewhere, or keep `skills` at the root while nesting the rest. The milestone's wording-mechanism decision avoided this kind of implicit rule.

No new settings key, and no resolution base in the tree. The `dangling-plugin-root` check takes each `<plugin_root>/<path>` reference and checks that `<path>` names a file `core/` holds that the host does not exclude. In other words, it checks the reference against the source layout that `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}` references are written in, not against the rendered tree. All hosts use this one rule. The docstring line is reworded to match, and the "build stays unchanged" clause is amended to cover this check. The check stops depending on where a host places its plugin inside the tree, so it works unchanged for a root plugin, a nested plugin, or any later layout. No definition or key changes. The check no longer proves that the rendered tree has the file at the path the runtime variable resolves to. A layout value or a `renames` entry that moves a referenced file away from its core-relative position would pass the gate and then fail at runtime. Today's check exists to catch exactly that, so this weakens it for all three hosts, not only Codex.

No new settings key and no derived base. A reference passes when the rendered tree holds a file whose path is exactly `<path>` or ends in `/<path>`, under any directory. All hosts use this rule. For Claude Code and Antigravity it reduces to today's behaviour, because their files sit at the root. The docstring line is reworded, and the "build stays unchanged" clause is amended to cover this check. The change is the simplest possible edit: one comparison in the check, nothing in the definitions or the settings schema, and no rule about where the plugin root sits. The check gets looser in a way that is hard to notice. A reference can pass because a matching file sits somewhere other than the plugin root, for example a root-level template or a second copy. So for Codex the gate no longer shows that `${PLUGIN_ROOT}/<path>` resolves at runtime. It catches only a path that names no file anywhere in the tree.

The dangling-reference check is not run for Codex. The build gains a per-host switch, for example a boolean settings key that every definition declares, false for Codex and true for the others. The check is skipped where the switch is off, and Codex's `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` references are first tested by the milestone's live verification. All other checks still run on the Codex tree. The docstring records the exemption. No resolution logic changes, and nothing has to be decided about how a nested plugin root is described. The two existing hosts keep today's check exactly. The live verification runs every tool call and shared-procedure read through `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` anyway, so a broken path shows up at the latest there. Codex is the only host whose broken plugin-root references reach the committed tree and every later `--check` without being caught. The gap is permanent: a future `core/` edit that leaves a dangling reference passes CI for Codex and surfaces only when a Codex user runs the skill. The only Codex verification the milestone runs is a small free-tier one. It still adds a settings key and a build change, just to turn the check off.

open-question.question: The live verification mixes runner-executed checks (the plugin install and two headless agent dispatches) with one check the maintainer must run by hand in an interactive session, and a headless complete-all-tasks run has no one to pause for. How is the maintainer's interactive check placed relative to the task list?
open-question.recommendation: The whole verification is derived into the initial batch, so the maintainer's check is listed in TASKS_TODO.md and no clean end-of-run report can hide it. The three runner outcomes are committed at a task boundary before the pause, so the dispatches never run twice and a quota stop resumes from committed state. A FAILED at that task is accurate, not a disguise: the task's bar is unmet until the maintainer has run the check, and the commit the inline skill leaves in the workspace is the evidence the second run reads.
open-question.alternative: The interactive check is its own task, the last one in the initial batch. It comes right after a runner verification task that does the plugin install and the two headless agent dispatches, records those three outcomes in TASKS_DONE.md, and keeps the temporary workspace. The brief of the interactive-check task says it passes only when the workspace shows that the maintainer ran the inline skill interactively, such as the commit that skill leaves in the workspace's git history. It also says the completer must never run the skill itself. A headless complete-all-tasks agent finds no such evidence and returns FAILED, so the loop stops there. The maintainer then runs the check by hand in an interactive Codex session and runs the task again with complete-task or complete-all-tasks. That run checks the workspace evidence, records the fourth outcome, and deletes the workspace. derive-tasks writes the whole verification into the initial batch, so the maintainer's step is listed in TASKS_TODO.md and can't be forgotten. The pause lands exactly between the runner's checks and the maintainer's. Because the dispatches sit in an already-completed task, they are never run twice, which keeps the "each still runs exactly once" rule and the free-tier quota safe. It uses FAILED as a planned pause, so the run reports a real failure for an expected stop, and nothing in the report tells the two apart. The headless agent might also try to produce the evidence itself, for example by running the skill through codex exec, which would break the split between modes and spend a scarce model call. Only the brief's wording prevents that. Using a commit in the workspace as evidence works only if the chosen inline skill commits anything, and the sibling question "Verification inline skill" decides which skill that is.

All four checks sit in one verification task, the last one in the initial batch. The headless complete-all-tasks agent does the install and both headless dispatches. When it reaches the interactive check it returns FAILED, leaving the three outcomes as resumable partial work: uncommitted changes in the cairn tree plus the kept temporary workspace. The maintainer runs the interactive check by hand. A second run of the same task picks up the partial work, adds the maintainer's check from the workspace evidence, and writes all four outcomes as one TASKS_DONE.md entry. All four outcomes land in one TASKS_DONE.md entry under one Task-completion commit, which matches the run-mode decision's "records all four outcomes" in the simplest shape. The task list also stays one task shorter. Between the two runs, the three runner outcomes exist only as uncommitted partial work. If the resumed completer misreads them, it runs the dispatches again, spending the scarce free-tier quota and breaking "each still runs exactly once". The quota-exhaustion rule of "pick up at the first unrun check" then depends on reading that partial state, not on committed task boundaries. It shares the FAILED-as-pause cost, and the commit-evidence condition on the sibling question "Verification inline skill", with the designed-stop option.

The initial batch ends with the runner verification task: install plus the two headless dispatches, with the three outcomes recorded in TASKS_DONE.md and the temporary workspace kept. The interactive check is in no task. The maintainer runs it by hand after complete-all-tasks finishes cleanly. A follow-up task is then added through submit-task. It records the fourth outcome, checked against the workspace's evidence plus the maintainer's observation written into its brief, and deletes the workspace. This is the same after-the-batch follow-up path the contradiction-handling decision already uses. No task is designed to fail, the headless run ends on its normal success line, and every task in the batch can be done fully unattended. The maintainer's step reuses an existing path, follow-up tasks via submit-task, so no new convention is needed. The maintainer's step appears nowhere in TASKS_TODO.md, so only the maintainer's memory of the milestone keeps it from being skipped. "All tasks completed." is printed while one required check hasn't run. The follow-up task is written after the fact by the person whose check it records, not derived with the batch. Its evidence again depends on the inline skill leaving a trace in the workspace, and the sibling question "Verification inline skill" decides which skill that is.

The initial batch holds no verification task, and complete-all-tasks runs it headless to the end. Afterwards a single verification task is added through submit-task and completed inline with complete-task in an interactive cairn session. That runner does the install and runs both dispatches as headless codex exec runs. It then asks the maintainer to run the interactive Codex check, waits in the conversation for the result, confirms it against the workspace, and records all four outcomes in one TASKS_DONE.md entry. The check happens inside the task that records it, so no designed failure is needed, and all four outcomes still land in one entry. The runner can ask the maintainer directly and follow up on an unclear result in conversation instead of guessing from leftover files. The complete-task procedure has no step for waiting on a person, so the pause depends on the inline runner choosing to ask. The same task run through complete-all-tasks would have no one to ask. The verification is missing from the derived batch, so its existence again depends on the maintainer remembering to submit it. A long single task that waits on a person also has no committed checkpoint if the quota runs out partway.

This rejects the premise of a headless run. The whole task list, including a final verification task that holds all four checks, is completed by the maintainer with complete-task, one task at a time, in an interactive cairn session. complete-all-tasks is not used for this milestone. When the verification task reaches the interactive check, the runner pauses for the maintainer, takes the outcome from the conversation and the workspace, and records all four in one entry. Every task, the verification included, is derived into the initial batch and run by someone who can be asked. No task fails by design and none is added later. It gives up unattended completion for the whole milestone just to handle one step. The maintainer has to drive every task of a long batch by hand. Nothing in the list stops a later complete-all-tasks call from reaching the verification task headless, where it has no one to ask.
